name: Blueprint
description: Review an agent's plan before it touches a file. The agent publishes its plan over MCP; Blueprint parses the markdown into addressable blocks and renders it next to a dependency graph derived from the steps' own `depends_on` edges — so the two questions a wall of markdown cannot answer become visible at a glance: what actually has to happen first, and which step is the one everything else is waiting on. A plan reads as a sequence because prose is a sequence; the work almost never is. You annotate what you object to, anchored to the block or step it belongs to — a comment, a redline carrying the replacement text you want, a question, or a blocker — and then approve or request changes. The verdict is not a mood: it is a document. Requesting changes serializes every annotation into deterministic text the agent reads back through `blueprint.plan_status`, each finding naming the step or block it attaches to and, for a redline, the exact substitution proposed, so a revision answers what was actually written rather than what a summary of it sounded like. Re-publishing under the same plan id appends a revision instead of creating a new plan, and block ids are content-stable across revisions, so the second draft arrives as a diff against the first — the paragraphs you already read are still the paragraphs you already read.
tagline: Read the plan as a graph, mark it up, and send back a verdict the agent can act on

blueprint.description: Publish a plan for a human to review, and read the verdict back as text. Reach for this before a change that is expensive to undo — a migration, a refactor across many files, anything where the wrong first step wastes the rest. `plan_publish` posts numbered steps with their `depends_on` edges and returns a review url; `plan_status` polls for the verdict with a bounded wait and returns the reviewer's annotations already serialized into readable findings; `plan_get` fetches the whole plan with its annotations; `step_update` marks a step done as the work lands, so the reviewer watching the graph sees progress without being asked.

hook_events.title: A plan was published for review
hook_events.description: A revision was written and the plan is now `in_review`. Fires on EVERY publish, including a re-publish under an existing `plan_id` — that is a new revision of the same plan, not a new plan, so a listener sees one event per revision and not one per plan. Use `revision` to tell a first draft (1) from a response to a verdict (2 and up). Does NOT fire when someone annotates a plan or when a step's status changes; annotations and step progress do not create revisions.

hook_events.title: A plan was approved
hook_events.description: A reviewer recorded an `approved` verdict against a specific revision. This is the signal that an agent blocked on review may begin editing. Fires only when a verdict is posted — resolving every annotation on a plan is not a verdict, and a plan with no annotations at all is not approved by default. `note` is the reviewer's free text and is often absent; approval never depends on it. Unresolved `comment` annotations may still exist on an approved plan, and are carried into the feedback text as advisory.

hook_events.title: A reviewer asked for changes
hook_events.description: A reviewer recorded a `changes_requested` verdict. `annotation_count` is how many annotations were open on that revision when the verdict landed — it is a size hint for a router deciding where to send this, not a list, and the annotations themselves are read back through `blueprint.plan_status`. Does NOT fire when a single `blocker` annotation is created: an unsubmitted blocker is one reviewer's opinion mid-read, and firing on it would page someone before the reviewer had finished forming a view.

hook_events.title: A plan step was marked done
hook_events.description: A step's status was set to `done`, normally by the agent calling `blueprint.step_update` as the work lands. Fires once per transition into `done`; the other statuses do not fire it, so moving a step to `in_progress` or `blocked` is silent and a step that goes `done` is not reported again by later updates that leave it there. This is the event to hang progress notifications on — it is the only one that means work actually happened, as opposed to work being agreed.
